# Do I need to bleed all 4 brakes if I only opened one line?

In hydraulic brake systems, the fundamental unit is a closed loop designed to transmit pressure uniformly across all wheels. When you work on the system, you are essentially introducing air into that loop. Air bubbles act as compressible cushions; under pedal application, they absorb energy rather than transmitting it to the friction material. The goal of bleeding is to evacuate this compressible volume and restore the direct hydraulic coupling between the master cylinder and the wheel cylinders or calipers.

The short answer to your specific scenario—replacing crush washers on a banjo bolt after a full flush—is that you should re-bleed the entire system, not just the single line you opened. While it might be tempting to isolate the repair zone and assume the rest of the fluid remains pristine, the physics of hydraulic systems dictate otherwise.

### The Nature of Hydraulic Contamination

When you disconnect any component in a master-cylinder-fed loop, you break the seal between the reservoir and the downstream components. Even if your brake lines were pressurized with clean fluid moments before disassembly, the moment that connection is severed, atmospheric air immediately enters the lowest point of that section. Air has a much lower density than brake fluid and will naturally rise to the highest points in the disconnected section when gravity or pedal pressure is applied.

If you only re-bleed the line where the leak was fixed (the rear left), you are removing air from that specific branch. However, there is no guarantee that the entire system is now void of entrapped air pockets elsewhere. Air can become trapped in high spots within the brake lines or inside the master cylinder reservoir itself if the fluid level dropped during the initial work and wasn't perfectly maintained.

### The Risk of Cross-Contamination

Consider the flow path from the master cylinder to your rear left caliper. To get air out of that specific line, you must force clean fluid through it to push the bubbles toward a bleed valve or vent hole. If there is any residual air in the section leading up to that line—perhaps near the ABS modulator (if equipped) or at other wheel cylinders—that air will not be expelled by bleeding just one caliper. The compressed air pocket upstream acts as a barrier, preventing clean fluid from clearing the entire path.

Furthermore, if the master cylinder was drained even slightly during your initial flush to accommodate the new hardware, the reservoir likely sucked in some air before being topped off again. This creates a scenario where the source of the pressure (the master cylinder) is no longer "perfect." Bleeding one line assumes the source is perfect; it does not account for potential contamination at the origin point.

### Best Practices for System Integrity

The industry standard and the most reliable method to ensure safety is to treat any breach in the hydraulic integrity as a system-wide event. If you have already performed a full flush, the fluid quality is optimal throughout the entire loop. Re-bleeding all four wheels takes only a few extra minutes but guarantees that no air pockets remain anywhere in the circuit.

If you choose to skip bleeding the untouched lines and encounter a spongy pedal or uneven braking later, diagnosing whether it's an old bubble trapped upstream versus a new leak downstream becomes difficult. The cost of time spent troubleshooting far exceeds the initial effort of a complete re-bleed.

In professional environments, this approach is often automated or standardized to eliminate human error. For example, in software deployment pipelines, if one node fails during a critical update, the entire cluster is rolled back and redeployed rather than attempting to patch just the failed instance without verifying the integrity of the shared dependencies. Similarly, in brake systems, the "shared dependency" is the hydraulic fluid itself; if any part of the circuit was compromised or potentially contaminated by air ingress, the safest assumption is that the whole system requires verification.

### Final Recommendation

Since you have already replaced the crush washers and reopened the banjo bolt connection on the rear left caliper, you are now in a state where the hydraulic integrity has been broken again. The most prudent course of action is to re-bleed all four wheels using a vacuum bleeder or pressure bleeder connected to the master cylinder reservoir. This ensures that any air introduced during the banjo bolt replacement, as well as any potential air drawn into the reservoir during your initial work, is completely purged from the system before you take the vehicle back on the road.
